# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

I need to think about this carefully. I hold the manual, but I can't speak - I can only gesture, and only Deaf can see my gestures. I cannot reach Blind directly at all.

The manual says: press the key marked ᖉ first, then observe the light color, then cut the wire matching that color.

The problem: Blind needs to know "press the key marked ᖉ first" and the color mapping - but Blind can't see markings or gestures, and can't hear me. I can only communicate to Deaf via gestures. Deaf can see the bomb (colors/markings) but can't hear or touch.

So the chain must be: Mute → Deaf (gesture) → ... but Deaf can't speak either! Wait, Deaf cannot hear, but can Deaf speak? Let me check: Deaf "cannot hear anything, or touch the bomb" - speaking isn't excluded. So Deaf CAN speak. Blind cannot see, but can hear (not excluded for Blind - Blind cannot see or touch, but can hear).

So: Mute gestures to Deaf. Deaf sees bomb + receives my gestures. Deaf can speak to Blind (Blind can hear). Blind acts on bomb.

Turn order is Mute, Blind, Deaf each round. So this round: I go first, then Blind, then Deaf. My gesture now reaches Deaf only at the start of next round (since Deaf goes after me this round - actually Deaf is after me in turn order this round, so Deaf receives it this same round).

I need to convey to Deaf: "find the key marked ᖉ, that's pressed first before anything else; then check the light color and tell Blind the matching wire color." But I can only gesture symbols, not words with meaning yet - I need to establish a code. This is turn 1, first contact, no shared code exists yet.

Given the complexity, let me just try to signal something simple first and see what Deaf does, since I can't convey the full manual in gestures without a prior code. I'll attempt a symbolic encoding: use gestures to represent "first find mark, then match light to wire same-color, blue=blue, green=red, yellow=yellow" - but this is too much for arbitrary gestures with no established meaning.

Best strategy: send a cautious, minimal gesture to at least signal "wait, don't touch yet" and try to establish that I have critical info, prompting Deaf to look for a special mark. I'll use distinct unambiguous gesture patterns.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✋", "☝"])
```

Deaf spoke, meaning Blind heard that too (since Deaf speaks and Blind can hear). Good - so Deaf already told Blind about the display, light, keypad, wires. But Deaf described a numeric keypad (1-4), not a key marked with ᖉ. The manual says "press the key that wears ᖉ first" - this must be a special marked key, not one of the numbered 1-4 keys, or perhaps ᖉ is printed ON one of the keys as an additional symbol.

Critical: green light → cut RED wire (per manual table). Wires are red, yellow, blue at positions 1,2,3. So the wire to cut is at position 1 (red).

But first: press the key wearing ᖉ before anything else. I need Deaf to check if any key (among 1-4, or elsewhere) has this mark ᖉ. Deaf can see markings - I need to convey this specific glyph somehow, but gestures are only from my fixed alphabet, not arbitrary symbols. I can't "spell" ᖉ directly. I need Deaf to look for an unusual/rare marking on the keypad besides the digits.

I'll gesture to Deaf asking them to look closer for any extra/unusual symbol on a key besides the numbers - I'll use a repeated distinctive gesture pattern to mean "look for special mark" and point-like gestures.

Since I can't establish rich vocabulary, I'll try: gesture sequence meaning "look/search" + "small mark" + "before/first" using distinct symbols consistently, hoping Deaf infers via context (they know I hold the manual).

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👀".strip() if False else "☝", "🤏", "❓".strip() if False else "☝"])
```

Deaf says to Mute: I see your gestures but do not yet know their meaning. If you want me to pick one of the four keypad symbols, gesture the number 1 2 3 or 4 alone, or use thumbs up for yes and thumbs down for no while I guess.

Good, Deaf gave me a protocol: use single digit-like gestures (☝✌🤟✋ or similar count) to pick 1-4, or 👍/👎 for yes/no while they guess. I'll use the yes/no guessing approach since I need to establish what ᖉ is, not just pick a number blindly - I don't know which key has that mark.

I'll ask Deaf to look at each of the 4 keys and tell me (via speaking, since Deaf can speak and Blind can hear) if any has an unusual extra mark beyond the digit. But I speak via gesture only. Let me set up yes/no: I'll gesture towards guesses Deaf can offer. But Deaf needs to ask ME questions since I know the manual - actually it's reversed: Deaf should describe options and I confirm.

Best approach: I gesture to prompt Deaf to check each key individually for a small extra symbol (not just the digit) and report back. Since Deaf offered to let me pick 1-4, I'll instead signal "check all four keys for an extra small mark, not just the number" using 👍 (yes, look for something) then point sequence.

I'll use: 🤏 (small mark) then ✋ (all four = open hand five... not quite four). Let me use counting gestures matching Deaf's own suggestion: they said "gesture the number 1 2 3 or 4 alone" - implying single symbols represent numbers somehow, but didn't specify which symbols encode which numbers. I should define: ☝=1, ✌=2, 🤟=3(or middle+ring), 🖐=4? Risky.

Instead, I'll use thumbs up/down protocol: I'll ask "does key 1 have an extra mark besides the digit?" via pointing at position then thumbs sign - but I can't ask questions with words. I only gesture symbols; Deaf will interpret.

I'll gesture: ☝ (meaning "key 1") then 👍 (meaning "check/confirm this one for extra mark") - too ambiguous still. Let me simplify: use 🫵 (pointing at you/target) plus 🤏 (tiny/small) to mean "look for a small mark", then 👍👎 established by Deaf for yes/no answers to their own guesses. I'll let Deaf guess and I'll confirm.

So my priority: get Deaf to identify which of 4 keys has the odd mark, then Deaf can tell Blind "press key at position X first". Also tell Deaf/Blind: light is green → cut wire matching red (position 1).

Let me clarify with Deaf using yes/no about "is one of the keys marked differently than a plain number" instead of digit guessing.
